charts.label: Sources of Company Value by Driver of Valuation

description.en: This factor evaluates the originality, uniqueness, diversity of application scope, technological coverage, and industry influence of the company's technology. Technologies with higher novelty and the ability to achieve breakthroughs and expansion in scientific development and application scenarios usually possess greater potential economic and technological value (Fu et al., 2026; Bessen, 2008; Fischer & Leidinger, 2014). Technological novelty contributes 47% to the valuation, indicating that this factor is one of the important determinants of company valuation. Changes in technological originality, patent filing strategy, application scope, or industry influence may play a relatively significant role in valuation enhancement or adjustment.
description.zh: 该因素评估企业技术的原创性、独特性、应用范围多样性、技术覆盖度和行业影响力。具有较高新颖性，并能够在科学发展和应用场景中实现突破与扩展的技术，通常具备更高的潜在经济和技术价值（Fu 等，2026；Bessen，2008；Fischer & Leidinger，2014）。技术新颖性在估值中贡献比例为47%，说明这一因素是影响企业估值的重要因素之一。技术原创性、专利布局、适用范围或行业影响力的变化，将对估值提升或调整产生较为明显的作用。

description.en: This factor evaluates how the company's stage in the technology life cycle affects valuation, including technological maturity, industrialisation progress, and future development trajectory (Fu et al., 2026; Taylor & Taylor, 2012; Tipping et al., 1995). In general, technologies at more advanced R&D stages, close to or already entering industrialisation, and with a clear growth path tend to have greater potential economic value. Technology life cycle accounts for 3% of the valuation, indicating that this factor has a relatively limited impact in the current valuation structure. Advancement in the R&D stage, improvements in technological maturity, and changes in future development stages remain important to overall valuation, but their impact is limited, and company value depends more on the performance of other dimensions.
description.zh: 该因素评估企业技术发展阶段对估值的推动作用，包括技术成熟度、产业化进展以及未来发展态势(Taylor & Taylor, 2012; Tipping et al.,1995)。通常而言，处于更高级研发阶段，接近或进入产业化，并具备明确成长路径的技术和企业，往往具有高的潜在经济价值。技术生命周期在估值中占比3%，说明这一因素在当前估值结构中的影响相对较小。研发阶段的推进、技术成熟度的提升以及未来发展阶段的变化，对整体估值很重要，但是影响有限，企业价值的提升更多取决于其他维度的表现。

description.en: This factor evaluates the application potential of the company's technology in the target market, including market size, demand intensity, growth expectations, and competitive landscape. Technologies that address large markets, benefit from clear demand growth, and possess a certain degree of technological barriers usually offer greater upside in company valuation (Fu et al., 2026; Kalcheva et al., 2018; Vega-González et al., 2010). Market factors account for 10% of the valuation, indicating that this factor has a certain influence on valuation, but it is not the primary determinant. Changes in market size, demand, or the competitive landscape may affect valuation to some extent, while company value is still jointly shaped by other dimensions.
description.zh: 这一因素评估企业技术在潜在市场中的应用空间，包括市场规模、市场需求强度、增长预期以及竞争格局等情况。通常市场规模较大、需求增长明确、且具有一定技术壁垒的技术和企业，其估值更具提升空间(Kalcheva et al., 2018; Vega-González et al., 2010)。市场因素在估值中占比10%，对企业估值具有一定影响，但并非主要决定因素。市场规模、需求变化或竞争格局的调整，可能对估值产生一定作用，同时企业价值仍受到其他维度因素的共同影响。

description.en: This factor evaluates how the team's capabilities in technological innovation, R&D investment, commercialisation, and risk management affect company valuation. It also assesses the risks and uncertainties associated with technological protection, rights stability, and potential competitive risks in the market (Fu et al., 2026; Boone et al., 2019; Damanpour & Schneider, 2006; Gans et al., 2008). Teams with strong R&D capability, stable execution, and sound risk management mechanisms are generally better positioned to realise the value of the company's technology. Team characteristics and risk contribute 40% to the valuation, indicating that this is an important factor affecting company valuation. Changes in team capability, technological protection, or external competitive risks may influence the valuation outcome to a considerable extent.
description.zh: 该因素评估企业团队在技术创新、研发投入、成果转化、以及风险管理等方面的能力，同时考虑技术保护、权力稳定性、潜在竞争风险以及不确定性等因素对企业价值的影响（ Boone et al., 2019; Damanpour & Schneider, 2006; Gans et al., 2008）。具备较强研发能力、稳定执行能力以及完善风险管理机制的团队，通常更有能力降低风险和不确定性，实现企业技术价值。团队特征与风险在估值中贡献40%，说明这是影响企业估值的重要因素。团队能力、技术保护状况或外部竞争风险的变化，可能在较大程度上影响估值结果。

children.text: In accordance with applicable valuation laws, regulations, standards and normative requirements, and following objective, independent, impartial and scientific principles, OxValue's valuation methodology was applied to estimate the value of the commissioned project. Subject to the assumptions and limitations set out in this report, the valuation result of the commissioned project is as follows:

Technological Novelty, Technology Life Cycle, Market, and Team Characteristics and Risk contribute 47%, 3%, 10%, and 40% to the company valuation, respectively. Overall, company valuation is relatively more sensitive to changes in Technological Novelty and Team Characteristics and Risk. Improvements or declines in the relevant indicators may have a more noticeable impact on future valuation. By contrast, Technology Life Cycle and Market remain important dimensions in assessing company value, but changes in their indicators tend to have a relatively smaller impact on overall valuation fluctuations.

cells.text: This valuation estimate is based on project, patent and product information provided by the client or relevant parties. The conclusion only reflects the value of the relevant assets included within the valuation scope and does not cover other intangible assets such as trade secrets, know-how or brands.

cells.text: Risk of Unclear Chain of Title

The patent has co-owners, making the title relationship comparatively complex. This may lead to coordination difficulties among co-owners, unclear benefit allocation, and constraints on unilateral disposal, thereby affecting title stability, transaction efficiency, and downstream disposal security.
A Single Patent Has Been Assigned More Than 3 Times

A single patent has undergone multiple assignments, making the chain of title comparatively complex. Potential issues may include defects in historical assignment procedures, unclear provenance of predecessor rights, or anomalous assignment consideration, which may affect title stability and increase the difficulty of title review and due diligence.
Patent Has Been Exclusively Licensed Out

The patent has been granted under an exclusive licence to external parties. During the licence term, the right holder loses the rights to self-implementation and further licensing, which affects subsequent industrialisation pathways and commercial revenue arrangements.
Risk over Title in Technology Sourcing or Collaborative Development
Collaborative Invention Patent Applications with Industry-Academia-Research Parties Exist

Patents jointly applied for with universities or research institutes may involve co-ownership of rights, unclear benefit allocation, or restrictions on subsequent use. Priority review should focus on industry-academia-research cooperation agreements, determination of service inventions, and whether subsequent commercialisation requires consent from cooperating parties.

The company obtains external patent usage rights by licence and does not itself hold title. Changes in licence term, licence fee, and licence status may affect sustainable technology use and cost structure, while also affecting assessments of technological autonomy and controllability.

Part of the company's technological capability derives from assigned external patents. Attention should be paid to the fit between assigned patents and the company's core business, fairness of assignment consideration, related-party relationship with the assignor, and whether there are 'window-dressing' assignments used to embellish technological strength.
Assigned Invention Patents Account for More Than 30%

The company's patent assets rely heavily on external technology inputs, and its independent R&D capability and technological independence may be insufficient. Attention should be paid to the fit between assigned patents and the principal business and their actual support for core competitiveness.
Risk of Dependence on Core Inventors
Invention Patents Contributed by the Top Three Inventors Account for More Than 80%

The company's invention patents are highly concentrated among a small number of core inventors, indicating that core technology formation and patent value creation are strongly dependent on key personnel. If core inventors leave or cooperative relationships change, this may affect technological continuity, patent portfolio stability, and valuation foundations.
Risk of Insufficient Patent Protection Term
Average Remaining Term of Protection for Invention Patents Is Less Than 5 Years

The company's core patent portfolio has entered the later stage of the term of protection, with a relatively short remaining exclusivity period. The period during which excess returns can be sustainably generated is therefore limited. As patents successively expire, related technologies may enter the public domain, and the company's technological barriers, market exclusivity, and upper bound of patent asset valuation may be materially affected.
Risk of Imbalanced Patent Portfolio Structure
The proportion of granted invention patents in total granted patents over the past three years is below the peer-domain average

The company's patent portfolio has a relatively low proportion of invention patents with high technological content and strong protection attributes. The portfolio structure may be skewed towards utility models and industrial designs, which generally provide comparatively weaker protection intensity. Insufficient reserves of invention patents may affect assessments of technological advancement, innovation capability, sci-tech attributes, and patent asset valuation.
Risk of Low Patent Application Quality
Invention patent grant rate is below the peer-domain average

The quality of invention patent applications, maturity of technical solutions, professionalism of patent drafting, or capability in prosecution responses may be insufficient. Core technologies may therefore be difficult to convert consistently into granted rights, which may affect technological protection capability, sci-tech attribute assessments, and patent asset valuation.
Risk of Limited Support from Patent Assets
No reserve of high-value invention patents has been formed

The company lacks a reserve of high-value invention patents, indicating a comparatively weak quality and value foundation of patent assets. This makes it difficult to adequately demonstrate core technological leadership and market-entry barriers, and provides limited support for principal business development, sustained revenue generation, and company valuation uplift.
Risk of Insufficient Technological Innovation Momentum
Invention patent activity over the past three years is below the peer-domain average

The company's recent R&D input, technological output, or patent portfolio deployment cadence may have slowed, indicating insufficient innovation momentum and continuous iteration capability. This may affect growth assessments, sci-tech attribute determinations, and future enhancement of patent asset value.
Risk of Innovation Discontinuity among Core Inventors
Top 5 core inventors have produced no invention patent output in the past three years

Sustained innovation activity among key technical personnel is insufficient, and capabilities in subsequent technology maintenance, R&D iteration, and patent portfolio deployment may weaken. If accompanied by attrition of core personnel or reduced R&D investment, this may affect technological continuity, innovation capability assessments, and the future value of patent assets.
Risk of Interruption in Innovation Output
No invention patent grants have been obtained in the past three years

Recent innovation output is insufficient, and R&D achievements have not been effectively converted into stable granted patent assets. This may indicate a slowdown in R&D output, weak patent application quality, or insufficient continuity of technology iteration.
Risk of Insufficient Patent Market Validation

The company's patents have not yet undergone market validation, and their commercial value and industrial transformation capability have not been fully demonstrated. There remains uncertainty as to whether they can sustainably support principal business growth, form competitive barriers, and realise asset monetisation.
The technical field falls within a high-incidence domain for patent invalidation proceedings

Competition in this field is comparatively intense, and relevant patents are more likely to become targets of invalidation challenges initiated by competitors during implementation and commercialisation.
The technical field falls within a high-incidence domain for patent infringement litigation

During implementation and commercialisation, patents may face infringement assertions from others and may also enter complex litigation or arbitration procedures in rights-enforcement processes. A high-frequency litigation environment is usually associated with elevated legal and time costs, and may introduce operational uncertainty through injunction relief, damages exposure, or settlement pressure.
The field is active in standard-essential patents and patent pools

If the company's products or technical solutions involve domains dense with standard-essential patents, relevant patent licensing is typically unavoidable. The company may face risks such as stacked licences from multiple right holders, uncertainty in FRAND rates, passive positions in licensing negotiations, and injunction relief, thereby increasing commercialisation costs, compressing margins, and affecting realisation of patent asset value.

This report is based on the AI-driven valuation platform independently developed by OxValue.AI. The platform is grounded in the Utility Theory of Technology Value originally proposed by the OxValue.AI team (Fu & Liu, 2022; Fu et al., 2026), and combines this theory with proprietary data resources and AI algorithms to form a systematic analytical framework for identifying, analysing and estimating the value of technology companies.

Building upon the technology valuation framework, the OxValue.AI valuation model employs machine learning methods to train, calibrate and continuously optimise model parameters using large volumes of historical data, technical indicators and market information, thereby improving the model's ability to identify and fit the actual market value characteristics of companies.
The framework covers four key attributes of technology company value:

• Technological novelty: this examines the novelty, technical advancement, originality and technological influence of the technology, reflecting its innovation quality, technical level and relative competitive position within the relevant technical field.

• Technology lifecycle: this analyses the development stage, maturity and future evolution trend of the technology, and assesses its current technological development level, room for subsequent iteration and potential for sustained application.

• Size of technological utility (market): this refers to potential application scope, target market size, competitive landscape and market activity, reflecting industrialisation prospects, market conversion capability and value realisation potential.

• Team characteristics and risks: this covers company team characteristics, technology-related risks and risk-management capability, and affects technology quality, diffusion and commercialisation outcomes, long-term feasibility and value creation.

Compared with traditional valuation approaches such as the cost approach, income approach and market approach, the OxValue.AI valuation model places greater emphasis on systematically analysing the multidimensional attributes that influence technology and company intrinsic value through a data-driven approach. Traditional methods often rely on historical costs, income projections, expert judgement or relatively isolated econometric models, whereas the OxValue.AI model is not limited to technology-specific features and further incorporates key dimensions such as technology lifecycle stage, team characteristics, commercial enablement conditions and related risk factors.

By combining big data, artificial intelligence and integrated econometric analysis, the model can evaluate and estimate the value of technology companies in a systematic and comprehensive manner. This AI-driven valuation approach significantly improves the objectivity, accuracy, efficiency, stability, reproducibility and interpretability of valuation results, thereby providing more scientific and reliable decision support for technology transactions, investment and financing decisions, and corporate strategic management.

In the EP region, the company’s head IPC main group is G09B23, covering models for scientific, medical, or mathematical purposes. The annual invention patent application data show an overall upward trajectory from 2005 to 2025, although the path is not linear. Patent counts increased from 23 in 2005 to 34 in 2006, followed by a period of fluctuation and moderate decline through 2010. A renewed expansion phase appeared from 2011 to 2014, with applications rising from 36 to 52, before a temporary pullback in 2015. From 2016 onward, the trend strengthened, reaching 75 applications in 2019, dipping to 67 in 2020, and then resuming growth to 95 by 2025. The 2022–2024 period suggests a near-plateau in applicant participation while patent filings continued to edge upward modestly.

Applicant counts broadly moved in line with patent counts, indicating that changes in filing volume were generally accompanied by corresponding changes in the number of participating applicants. This linkage is visible in the early rise from 2005 to 2006, the contraction around 2007–2010, the growth phase through 2014, and the later expansion from 2016 to 2022. However, the relationship was not perfectly proportional: applicant counts rose sharply to 93 in 2018 while patent counts reached 66, then declined in 2019 despite higher patent filings. In 2023–2025, applicant counts remained broadly stable or slightly lower, while patent counts continued to rise, suggesting a more concentrated increase in application activity within an applicant base that was no longer expanding at the same pace.

The annual data indicate a generally fluctuating but upward-leaning patent application profile over the observed period. A second expansion occurred in 2011–2012, reaching 84 applications, before another drop to 51 in 2013. From 2014 onward, filings moved into a higher activity band, with intermittent fluctuations: 80 in 2014, 92–94 in 2016–2017, a softer level in 2018–2019, and a later peak at 118 in 2023. Applicant counts broadly moved in the same direction as patent counts during several phases, particularly in 2006–2009, 2010–2012, 2020–2023, and the decline after 2023. However, the linkage was not uniform. For example, patent applications rose from 51 in 2013 to 80 in 2014 while applicant count increased only modestly from 116 to 135, and patent counts remained relatively high in 2016–2020 despite applicant counts staying well below the 2012 peak of 306. This indicates that PCT activity in G09B23 was shaped by both changes in the number of applicants and variations in filing intensity per applicant, with the later period showing comparatively higher patent volumes supported by a smaller applicant base than the early peak years.

After a temporary decline in 2011, both patent count and applicant count rebounded in 2012, and patent filings reached a local peak of 184 in 2014, while applicant counts remained elevated compared with the earlier period.

The smaller the TCT value, the more frequent the technological iteration, and the shorter the cycle of replacement of previous generation technologies; the larger the TCT value, the more stable the technology system, and the longer the sustained effective cycle of existing technological achievements.

The assessed company’s sector track is: healthcare and life sciences — medical education equipment and services — physical clinical and surgical simulation training devices, including task trainers, tissue/fluid simulation modules and related educational support, with a cautious linkage to software-enabled medical training platforms.

At the macro policy level, the 2023-2026 policy environment in the United Kingdom and broader European healthcare market has remained supportive of healthcare workforce expansion, patient safety improvement, clinical skills standardisation and technology-enabled medical education. Public health systems have faced sustained pressure from workforce shortages, training backlogs, elective care recovery and the need to improve procedural competency without increasing patient risk. Within this context, simulation-based education has been increasingly recognised as a practical tool for medical schools, hospitals and training centres to improve readiness before direct patient contact. Policy support is therefore indirect but material: funding priorities in healthcare capacity, education quality, digital learning and patient safety all reinforce demand for structured simulation tools rather than relying solely on apprenticeship-based clinical exposure. At the industry regulatory level, the company’s products sit at the intersection of educational equipment, medical training devices and, where applicable, software-supported learning. Physical simulators used for training are generally not equivalent to therapeutic medical devices, but manufacturers still need to address product safety, materials quality, infection-control compatibility, procurement documentation, data protection for any connected learning tools, and institutional requirements for repeatability and curriculum alignment. In the UK and EU, post-Brexit conformity assessment arrangements, product safety expectations and hospital procurement scrutiny have increased the importance of traceable design, quality management and robust technical documentation. For the enterprise, the policy environment is favourable but not subsidy-dependent. Limbs & Things benefits from structural public-sector demand for safer and more scalable clinical training, while also facing higher expectations on product reliability, evidence-based training outcomes and compliance readiness in cross-border sales. Overall, the policy dimension has a moderately positive impact on valuation by supporting resilient end-market demand and raising entry barriers, although the benefit depends on the company’s ability to maintain documented quality systems and adapt to evolving institutional procurement standards.

The identified niche is physical clinical and surgical simulation training devices, including task trainers that replicate anatomical structures, tactile feedback, procedural workflow and, in some cases, fluid behaviour. The current industry is moving from basic demonstration models toward more realistic, repeatable and curriculum-integrated training systems. Demand is driven by medical schools, nursing and midwifery programmes, surgical training centres, hospitals and continuing professional development providers seeking to reduce dependence on live patient availability and cadaver-based training. In this market, product value is determined less by simple manufacturing capacity and more by anatomical fidelity, durability, procedural relevance, ease of cleaning, replaceable consumables, educator usability and alignment with recognised clinical competencies. The key trend is the convergence of physical realism, modular training design and digital assessment. Institutions increasingly prefer simulation products that support standardised teaching scenarios, objective skills assessment, repeat use across learner cohorts and flexible configuration for different procedures. Hybrid models combining physical task trainers with online educational content, video guidance, sensor-based feedback or learning management integration are likely to gain relevance, although adoption varies by budget and teaching maturity. Another feature of the market is the shift from isolated device purchases to broader training solutions, including consumables, replacement parts, facilitator materials and scenario-based education packages. For Limbs & Things, the development trend is broadly favourable because its patent profile indicates accumulated know-how in surgical and clinical training devices, covers, fluid simulation and artificial tissue-related components. Such capabilities are aligned with customer demand for tactile, procedure-specific and repeatable training. The company’s valuation may therefore benefit from a technology and know-how premium if it can continue converting device-level innovation into scalable product families and recurring consumables. However, the valuation uplift should be assessed cautiously, as the pace of digital integration and outcome validation will influence whether the business is viewed as a specialised equipment manufacturer or a broader medical education platform.

The market space for clinical and surgical simulation training equipment is a specialised sub-segment within healthcare education and medical technology. It is smaller than the broader medical devices market but benefits from relatively stable institutional demand, because healthcare training cannot be fully deferred without affecting workforce supply and patient safety. Globally, the addressable market is best characterised as a billion-level opportunity when physical simulators, task trainers, related consumables, software-supported education and institutional training services are considered together. In the UK and European context, the market is narrower but supported by medical school enrolment, postgraduate clinical training, nursing and allied health education, and hospital-based skills centres. The demand base is fragmented across universities, health systems, private training providers and distributors, which limits single-customer concentration at the market level but also requires broad channel coverage. The principal growth characteristics are not explosive volume expansion but steady penetration of simulation into more procedures, earlier-stage education and continuing professional development. Demand is expanding from high-acuity surgical training into routine clinical skills, obstetrics, emergency care, primary care procedures and interprofessional team training. Institutions are also increasing emphasis on measurable competency before patient contact, which supports purchases of procedure-specific trainers and replacement consumables. Budget cycles remain a constraint, especially in publicly funded systems, but simulation equipment can be justified where it improves training throughput, reduces instructor burden or substitutes for scarce clinical exposure. For Limbs & Things, market space is attractive because its product orientation appears well matched to repeatable hands-on procedural training rather than one-off capital equipment alone. Consumables, replacement anatomical parts and refreshed course materials can improve lifecycle revenue if the installed base is actively managed. The company’s addressable space may be further broadened through international distribution and specialty-specific product extensions. Overall, the market-space dimension is positive for valuation, with the strongest support coming from resilient education demand and potential recurring product use, while the absence of a clearly dominant, rapidly scaling market size warrants a prudent revenue multiple rather than a high-growth software-style valuation framework.

children.text: The competitive landscape in clinical and surgical simulation training devices is specialised and multi-layered. At the high end, competition includes international medical simulation companies offering manikins, task trainers, virtual reality platforms and integrated training systems. In the mid-market, numerous specialist manufacturers compete in anatomical models, procedural trainers and discipline-specific simulation kits. At the local level, universities, hospitals and teaching centres may also use internally developed low-cost models or generic training aids for basic skills, which creates price pressure in less complex procedures. Competitive differentiation is therefore based on realism, procedural specificity, reliability, educator acceptance, after-sales support, availability of consumables and the ability to map products to curriculum requirements. The industry trend suggests increasing bifurcation. Premium suppliers are moving toward integrated simulation ecosystems that combine hardware, software, data feedback and structured scenarios, while cost-focused suppliers compete through simplified devices and regional distribution. For physical task trainers, intellectual property, proprietary materials, moulding techniques, fluid simulation design and anatomical know-how can provide defensible advantages, but these barriers are narrower than those in regulated therapeutic medical devices. Customer switching costs are moderate: once educators build lesson plans around a particular device family and keep spare parts or consumables in stock, repeat purchasing can be sticky, but new tenders may reopen competition. For Limbs & Things, the patent names indicate a focus on clinical and surgical training apparatus, medical simulation systems, covers, fluid simulation and artificial spinal disc or tissue-like compositions. This suggests a tangible product-innovation base that may support differentiation in hands-on realism and procedural use cases. The company’s competitive position will depend on breadth of catalogue, distributor reach, educator reputation, product lifecycle management and ability to respond to digital assessment trends. Overall, the competition dimension has a cautiously positive impact on valuation if the company demonstrates durable niche leadership and repeat customer relationships; however, valuation should reflect ongoing competitive pressure from larger integrated simulation vendors and lower-cost model manufacturers.

Risk identification for the company’s niche centres on five areas: public-sector education and healthcare budget pressure, product substitution by digital or lower-cost simulation formats, compliance and product quality expectations, intellectual property and materials know-how leakage, and channel dependence in international markets. Although simulation-based training is structurally supported by workforce and patient-safety needs, many customers operate under annual or multi-year procurement cycles, and discretionary capital purchases may be delayed during fiscal tightening. The company also faces technology risk if virtual reality, augmented reality or sensor-enabled platforms capture a larger share of training budgets in procedures where tactile realism is less critical. The transmission path is mainly through purchasing decisions and institutional curriculum design. If hospitals and universities shift budgets toward integrated digital platforms, or if low-cost alternatives are considered adequate for basic clinical skills, average selling prices and replacement cycles for physical trainers may weaken. Conversely, stricter procurement documentation, safety reviews or sustainability requirements could lengthen sales cycles and increase operating costs. Product defects, material durability issues or inconsistent simulation performance would directly affect educator trust and could lead to warranty costs, reputational damage or exclusion from repeat tenders. In export markets, changes in conformity assessment, distributor performance or logistics costs could further affect margins and customer service quality. The impact assessment is moderate rather than severe, because the core need for hands-on procedural training remains difficult to eliminate, particularly for skills requiring tactile feedback, instrument handling or fluid response. However, the company’s valuation should incorporate execution sensitivity around innovation cadence, quality systems, installed-base monetisation and channel resilience. The risk dimension therefore places a prudence discount on valuation multiples, partially offsetting the positive structural demand outlook, and makes evidence of repeat orders, product reliability and successful hybrid physical-digital positioning especially important in valuation assessment.

OxValue.AI is a leading vertical application in the field of AI-driven technology valuation. Its valuation model is built on nearly a decade of technology valuation research accumulated by Professor Xiaolan Fu, Fellow of the British Academy of Social Sciences and tenured Professor at the University of Oxford, and her team.

OxValue.AI is centred on the original Utility Theory of Technology Value (VEST) and has developed dedicated training datasets for valuation scenarios, together with a proprietary valuation database encompassing industry-specific valuation databases and foundation model databases. Through deep learning and model distillation techniques, the platform distils patterns from large volumes of historical valuation results and transaction data, and validates its models to produce industry-specific valuation algorithms tailored to different asset types, enabling accurate valuation across multiple scenarios. It has achieved intelligent valuation of patents, companies, innovation teams, data assets, and cultural IP, among other intangible assets, with more than ten thousand valuations completed to date, serving over 6,500 companies, and with deep deployment across diverse scenarios including equity investment, technology lending, technology insurance, technology transactions, technology transfer, government project review, and anti-fraud identification.

As a significant participant in the global technology valuation field, OxValue.AI's AI valuation technology has received high recognition from international organisations including WIPO and Innovate UK, and has been prominently recommended by the United Nations Technology Innovation Platform. Related research outputs and technology practices have been recognised by, among others, the European Academy of Management Best Paper Award (2017), the Falling Walls Science Breakthrough Award (2021), the University of Oxford Vice-Chancellor's Award (Innovation and Commercialisation Category — Special Commendation), the ASEAN Future Unicorn Award, and the Alibaba Cloud Global Summit Best AI Practice Award. OxValue.AI has contributed to the drafting of standards under the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, the Ministry of Science and Technology, and other bodies, with its valuation models and methodologies having been applied in standards development.
